title: The future of jazz
summary: Budd compares jazz to the airplane, a foundation that keeps growing, and approves of young players moving beyond one-chord rock.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Budd, just to sort of wind this up, we got a tremendous left --
Can you hold it a minute? Okay.

Budd, in sort of -- just one, this has been the most beautiful experiences I've ever had in my life, to sit with you, my old buddy, and just reminiscing and talking about some of the most beautiful things that occurred in your beautiful life and your contribution to this great American art form, jazz. Now can you, just in any kind of short way, whatever you feel, can -- what you think of, what do you think, what is the future of jazz?

Well, I think the future of jazz is very, very great. As you may notice, people are asking us to come to their universities to lecture, talk, and even demonstrate jazz. You yourself at Hunter College -- we have a lot of our friends throughout the colleges in the country. Clark Kerry's going around, all the guys. I think jazz is -- I can sum it up by saying something like this. The Wright brothers built the airplane. It's still the airplane. I don't

care. Now you're going to the moon, but it's still an airplane, and it just keeps progressing and going on and on and on and you have people that contribute more and more, and they learn more and more and add to it.

We have built a great foundation to be built upon, and I think jazz is like this. Jazz is going to be going on and on and on, I don't care what names people put on it, what they might want to call it.

It still comes from the roots. It's music, and basically it is that old music that we started to play, and maybe some call it -- they started off by saying ragtime and all of this stuff, but I mean you could take a guy that played a solo and put him behind a modern rhythm section, and it will still sound good, and it would fit.

It's a creative art form, and it's original, and anything that's original I don't think like that -- in arts -- will ever die, and it's just going on and on. And I just hope that some of the youngsters can keep this thing going and find an interest in it. All right, so they like rock and roll, rock and roll. Okay, we used to like rock and roll. We put it down, and we tried to go on further. I see that they're even improving on that. And some of the stuff I hear today the kids are playing is very

great. They're playing better music. They're off of that one and two chord stuff. They're going on and on and on, and they're getting closer to the things we played, all the old solos, and the electronic things may be a little different. I think it'll be here forever.
